utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usual question: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General Talic, good morning to you. Same question: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution? No one hiding today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No one is hiding. Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, and Denise Gustin, who will be returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Tania Radosavljevic together with lead counsel John Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, I am Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic together with Fabien Masson for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Yes, Ms. Korner? By the way, if there are no major hitches - and there shouldn't be - later on during the day we will be handing down the decision on the 90(H) motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very grateful, Your Honour. All I was about to say is that we filed yesterday - although it was after hours so it probably won't be filed until this morning actually - through the Registry the reply to the Rule 92 submissions made by Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau. We have combined the two together because Mr. Ackerman's was the principal and Madam Fauveau was the actual positive, if I can put it that way, objections to the particular statements. I can say straight away, Your Honours will -- and the Defence will see, if they have not already received it, in some cases we have made the decision that we will call the witnesses after all. In other cases, we are asking still that they be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen your response, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, I don't think it was filed until after the Registry shut but we just got it in so it will be filed this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then as far as the first proposal for the day is that I call Mr. Inayat to deal with the search of the radio station plus the analysis that he's done of the documents. I think Your Honours or the Registry have been given copies of a document that he's prepared. So perhaps you better have it now and then I'll ask for the investigator to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Ms. Korner, sorry to change the subject in such a fashion, but yesterday, we were handed a memorandum prepared by Mr. Ackerman in support of oral request for guidance as to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one we have responded to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the one. I didn't realise it was entitled "Memorandum."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I thought you were responding to some other document and I wanted to place because I could -- it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, if Mr. Inayat could come into court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please, could you bring Mr. Inayat in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are quite familiar with the procedure here. Please proceed to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know what you are here for, what's the purpose -- you're going to be asked some questions by Ms. Korner and then possibly by the Defence on the retrieval of documents from the Banja Luka Radio Station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner please proceed. Does he have a copy of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he does, he prepared this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, just for the record, could you give your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: My name is Mazhar Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you've already told the Court, you're in charge -- the team leader in charge of Team 1 which has been investigating this particular case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And yesterday, were you asked originally effectively from the Court to provide some information on the search of the Banja Luka Radio Station in -- on the 27th of February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was asked yesterday afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And originally did you use the internal report that was written by the person who conducted -- or the persons, I should say, who conducted that search but who no longer work for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read through his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And attached to his report is this -- or available to you was the -- what's called a field evidence register form, which is filled out, as you explained to us, I think, when you told us about the searches, at the scene to show what has been recovered.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I reviewed that particular document also, which is right in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact if one looks at it, is it right to say that it does not look as though any documents were seized relating to November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Apparently on the two pages, that precisely was my understanding, that November 1992 is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. However, did you as a result of a request made to you by myself yesterday conduct a survey of what exactly had been recovered from the Banja Luka Radio Station?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I was asked, and I have done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the document that has been handed to the Defence and to Their Honours. And if we just look at that, we can see extracting from it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment. I think just for record purposes, Your Honour, that this document needs to have some kind of a designation that would allow it to be identified in the record by someone who is reading it two years from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have taken it for granted that that will happen at some point in time. We don't need to take care of that from the very beginning. You know, we all know what document we are referring to at the present moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We do. But someone reading this transcript that's not here has no idea what we're talking about. I think it should be identified before -- that's up to Your Honours. It's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Ackerman. Your Honour, I'm not prepared to argue about this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we call that P516, please. It's entitled "Index - Banja Luka Radio Station documents, seized 27th of the 2nd, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you did, I think, was you went through the various boxes of material which were numbered, we can see, with the prefix of "Z," and not "Z." Then you went through the logs and showed the -- what's called the ERN range, which is the numbering of each document. And from that, you were able to see the numbering of entries, the total number of pages that it amounted to, the month, and the year. And if we look at that -- we can look at some of the oddities. But there were apparently some 26 separate documents amounting to 41 pages for January 1993. Then we see three -- two lines further on that there were four documents in this particular box relating to November 1992; then one document for October 1994 in that box. And then further down again -- I'm leaving out all the 1992s for the moment -- for October 1994, some 158 pages amounting to 39 documents were found. And then again two on, for November 1992, 109 documents amounting to just over -- or just under, really, 1200 pages. And then if we come down -- as I say, I'm leaving out 1992 because we have the majority for 1992. In the third box, Z25a, there were 284 documents relating to December 1991, one document for October 1991, 357 -- or 105 documents for January of 1991 - so nothing between January and October - and then 58 documents for November 1991. And again an oddity: There was one document for May of 1990 -- 1988. And then over on the next page, there were 11 documents relating to November 1989. And then we're back into 1992 again. And the total number of boxes of documents were four. There were effectively 8.993 documents altogether. And the total number of pages, just under 18.000. Is that correct, Mr. Inayat?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Total number of pages, I would suggest over 18.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I make that 17.840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the document that we have, Ms. Korner, we have 18.340.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm looking at a previous one. Sorry. Because there was a second -- that's right. Just over 18.000. And the total number of entries is still the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And from the record, it appeared - I think this is right, Mr. Inayat - that the radio station filing system was not of the greatest, putting it --

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, that is true, because according to the report of the investigator, the documents were piled up in a corridor against the wall and they had to sift through that material to find out the relevant months that were required. So yes, the filing wasn't what we're used to here in the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's asking for trouble. Thank you very much, Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman or Madam Fauveau, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Madam Fauveau will be asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Inayat, you personally were not present when documents were seized at Radio Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know exactly how the seizure took place.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Physically I was not present, but the report that I have looked at and the debriefings that I attended immediately - in fact, the same evening after the seizure happened - gave me enough information as to what procedures were used by the investigating team.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were all the documents in the radio building seized or was a selection made?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: According to the report of the investigator who was the leader in charge of the seizure, it appears -- there is a clear understanding in the document that they left behind a lot of material which wasn't considered relevant. There was a lot of material for the 1970s and 1980s, which of course wasn't considered relevant, and we didn't have the mandate to seize that material in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of which criteria were the documents you seized selected?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: We were clearly interested in the year 1992 and of course a few months before 1992 and a few months after 1992, because that was the time frame that we were looking at for our investigation purposes. So we knew very well that we have to focus on basically 1991, October onwards, until about January, February, March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: As regards 1992, did you take all the documents that you found for that year?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: As you can see from the evidence register form, which probably has been circulated also, the investigation team --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause. Your Honour, we have not. If anybody wants it, we can have the investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to have a look at it, Madam Fauveau and Mr. Ackerman? I personally don't think it's that important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a rough and ready list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I have to ask. I personally don't think it's of any relevance or importance, but you are entitled to see it, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not asking for it to be exhibited. It contains the names of a number of people who are no longer relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before undertaking the seizure of 1992 documents, did you have precise instructions regarding the contents of the documents or were your instructions to take all your documents dated -- all the documents dated 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: What I was about to point out about this evidence register form is that we got into this particular premises around about 8.00 in the evening, maybe slightly earlier, and the limited time -- in the limited time that we had, we just couldn't go through each and every document and make a selection there. We had about two or three persons who could speak the language, and the instructions were that anything that is relevant to the 1992 period must be collected. And so, in the limited time, of course, whatever was available for that period, we tried to seize it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you seized all the documents bearing dates in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: All documents that we were able to look into. As I said, this was -- radio station premises was spread over two buildings, and we weren't able to enter each and every room in the building. So whatever was available to us in that particular corridor on the second floor of the second building also numbered 129 on that particular street, so from that pile of documents, in the limited time, whatever we could find on 1992, we tried to seize that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in those 1992 documents that you considered to be relevant, there are about 500 pages concerning the Olympic Games, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Of course, if you look at the total seizure, they might not be all relevant. There are a lot of things in the 1992 period which are reportings on music programmes or concerts or different things which are certainly not relevant, but as I said, in those limited two hours that we had, we couldn't make a selection at that point of time. So I'm afraid there must be, as you point out, documents that are not relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope there are because otherwise we would have too many documents to look at, 18.360.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I meant was there might be a limited number of documents that are not relevant, because in the limited time we had, we couldn't select the relevant material right at that spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason for seizing documents from October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe anything that was seized for the period 1984 and also for 1989, those particular documents, as I can see from the logs, probably somehow got mixed up, because those particular documents don't appear separately on a different -- in a different folder. They were part of a folder of 1992 documents. So it is very much possible that these very few documents from 1989 and 1984, just by some mistake, I guess, found their way into these folders that were from the period 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your testimony that the report that was done after the seizure contained an error, specifically regarding the month of November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that certain documents seized were lost along the route from Banja Luka to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is -- in my personal opinion, that is out of the question, because the investigator who was responsible for this particular seizure, he has worked under me for almost like two years, and I have known him to be an extremely intelligent, diligent and a methodical person, and there is no chance of anything getting lost from his hands. I doubt that very much. And in any case, as soon as the seizures were completed, this particular investigator put everything in boxes and personally carried them to the holding area where we were staying, so they were never out of sight. So I'm afraid I just don't see that possibility at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is he the same person that drafted the report?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: He is the person who drafted the report, but let me point out, he is not the person who wrote the information on the evidence register form.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But he was the one who drafted the report, so he was the one who made the error?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: But he was following the information from this particular evidence register form, and I personally believe that he reported -- he wrote his report within days after the seizure had been completed. Being a non-native B/C/S speaker, being a -- he didn't know the B/C/S language, and so he didn't really have the time to go through the seized material to base his report, you know, for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the seized documents arrived in The Hague, is the same investigator the only person who was in touch with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: As soon as the documents were brought to the Tribunal, another investigator was appointed as a log manager, and this person, Mr. Hansen, the investigator who seized the material, had nothing to do with the logging process.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But when the documents arrived in The Hague, there were several people working with those same documents, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. There was one log manager, and he had a staff of several data entry clerks, data entry clerks who could speak the B/C/S language, and these data entry clerks then, after reviewing the documents, put -- inserted very brief summaries of what was contained in the document and also gave dates of the documents, in fact those logs I have used now yesterday to prepare this report that has been exhibited today. So yes, there were quite a few persons involved in creating these log sheets in English language.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much later after the arrival of the documents in The Hague the ERN number was attached to those documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I can find out the precise dates for you, because it's easy because the ERN ranges are here and I can very easily go to the evidence unit and find out the exact dates. But my recollection is that it was within weeks that the material seized from Banja Luka was passed on to the evidence unit, which was then responsible to stamp the ERN numbers on the documents. So it didn't take really very long. But if you are interested, I can get back to you and give you precise information as far as dates are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the documents were scanned on CD-ROMs before the ERN number was attached to them.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't believe that that is true. I think the documents were scanned into the system first, into the network, and it was later when we had to review the material with certain experts that we requested the evidence unit to please provide this material on CDs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Inayat, I ought to correct that because in fact they were scanned twice. There was a set scanned. And I believe the Defence had it without ERN numbers, and that's why the question is being asked. So there were two sets of scanning. But that's why the question is being asked. I don't think Mr. Inayat has even dealt with that part. But I can confirm that they were scanned originally without the numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, we received those documents without the ERN numbers. Does that mean that the documents without those numbers were scanned within a period of one week after their arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: The initial scanning that happened was with the unit numbers that the team was able to provide during the logging, because every folder had its own particular number. And I think again, this is something that I need to really check before I commit myself to giving you a correct answer on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to just now return to Banja Luka, please. When the seizure took place in the building of Radio Banja Luka, you said that you were not able to enter into all the premises.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the -- according to the report of the investigator, there were a few rooms - I would say about a couple of rooms - that were locked. So they -- according to that report, they were -- in the limited time they had, they were unable to visit each and every location of those two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the investigators try to enter these premises? Did they try to find the key or find the person who could perhaps open a door for them?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Probably I'll have to go back and read the report, because it was quite a long report, like, seven pages. I'm not so sure if that effort was made or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after the seizure took place at the building of Radio Banja Luka, you did not return to try and find other documents?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, two or three months later one of our colleagues from the Sarajevo field office was requested by the team to go back to Banja Luka and to obtain additional material from the SRT, from the Serb Radio and Television. And if my memory is serving me right, I think in April of 1998 the investigator did bring back additional material. But again, I would like to say that I have to check this information. But that investigator who conducted this seizure didn't go back, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is possible that the Prosecutor's office does have other documents from Radio Banja Luka, others than those contained on the list of the documents seized.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I really would have to check this before I commit myself to an answer on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this request from April 1998 also concerns the documents from 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have to go back and look at those documents to tell you if it is -- if those documents are actually pertaining to that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I have a few queries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I have questions, should they be after yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't realise you had. No, Mr. Ackerman, please go ahead first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you actually in preparation for your testimony today go through the CDs, the Z15, Z25, and Z27 that have been provided to us and look at those?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have access to this material on the network, so I didn't see it on the CD. But I did go through boxes Z15, 25, 25A, and 27. That's how I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "boxes," you're not talking about physical boxes but you're talking about material that's been scanned into the computer.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And that material is scanned into the Zy-lab document retrieval system, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that system and how it works and do you use it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I haven't used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how to conduct searches on it?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have done that a couple of times. But that was sometime ago, and new versions have now been introduced which I haven't been using.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know - and you perhaps don't - that some of the documents were apparently scanned twice and appear on those CDs more than once?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do all documents that come into the evidence unit of the Office of the Prosecutor get scanned into that Zy-lab document retrieval system?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the routine.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: I would imagine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Well, you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, do you actually know whether all documents that come into the Office of the Prosecutor are scanned in? If you don't, Mr. Inayat, say so.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: All documents that are seized definitely are scanned into the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What about if people send up documents unasked for?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: There is a possibility that sometimes they are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think, had some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the -- under the column "ERN range," does the letter "B" indication anything in particular? Does it refer to a box or something, or what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this prefix "B" is given to a ERN range for documents that were seized in Banja Luka. So "B" would always mean documents seized in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka. Now, can -- I see with regard to the radio station documents you have this sequence: B1, then B2, and then you have B5.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is there this break in a sequence? You don't have 3 and 4, and you have 5.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honours, since we had these boxes marked Z1 till probably Z40-something, these were taken out one at a time, and sometimes a box would come out from the CSB building, and so that would be scanned first. The other box could have documents for the SDS material. The third could be for the municipal building. So as the boxes were going to the evidence -- as the evidence unit was opening those boxes, they started giving those ERN numbers so as you can see there were four boxes for Banja Luka so they probably got scanned at different stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see five at least, B5?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Z15 -- I would assume that Z15 was one of those boxes which got scanned on very late and was assigned ERN numbers at a very late stage. Z25 which starts with B001 was scanned early on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I notice that between Z25 and Z25A, roughly halfway down the page, just before we start Z25A, last page seems to be B001-5034, and then Z25A, continues with B001-8759. This seems to be the only occasion on this chart, on this sheet, where this is so. Is there a reason for this? What happened to the -- do you have any information with regard to the documents which had pages B001-5035 to 8758?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, that again is very much possible that the documents found for that particular range came from a different box, and so before Z25A1 was being scanned, that particular -- the documents from that particular box probably got scanned in before. And so those numbers were assigned to the documents from that particular box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to tell me that in Banja Luka, for example, radio station, when the documents were seized, there is the possibility that these may have been mixed with documents recovered from other places?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. What I'm saying is that once these documents were brought to Banja Luka, they were contained in many boxes, and so one of the investigators, for making it more convenient that the boxes are transported to The Hague, he took out documents from boxes and put them in larger boxes. That's how the number of boxes were reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're not answering my question. It doesn't explain what happened or what may have happened to pages B001-5035 to B001-8758 because I would imagine that if these were being scanned as Banja Luka first batch, they were being scanned together. I mean, where do we find pages B001-5035 to B001-8758?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honours, those -- roughly speaking those 300 pages that are missing from these two areas that you have pointed out were also documents seized from Banja Luka and probably they were in a box that was a CSB box, document seized from the CSB, for example, or could have been documents seized from the municipal assembly. So as soon as Z25 was ERNed and ERN numbers assigned, and just before Z25A was to start, the evidence unit must have taken out the documents from that particular box that I'm trying to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think can I help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If someone can explain also, Ms. Korner, before you start, I also note that B001, unlike all the other batches or ranges, does not start with page 1. It starts with page 3.861.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is -- if I can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I want to have clear in my mind

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Inayat, is this the situation, that each of the boxes as they came from the various places that were searched, were marked? In other words, that box whatever it was would be marked Banja Luka Radio Station, CSB building for a different one? As you said, some of the smaller boxes were then placed into larger ones for transport to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are then given to the evidence unit who book them in?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To do this stamping process, what's called the ERN numbers, physically the boxes are given to a team of people who one by one take out the documents and stamp them with these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But because there is a team of people, one person may be just taking boxes as they are piled in front of them, one from the radio station, one from the CSB, and so that's why there is an interruption in this range of numbers?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour grasp that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I grasp it, but I find it strange to say the least, because it doesn't make sense. If you are organising the cataloguing and marking and whatever, you get the Banja Luka ones together and someone does -- or groups them together and keeps them together. As it is, it's not like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, it was -- as I understand the situation, I'm sorry, there were so many -- the boxes were simply piled up in front of these people who took out the papers one by one and went stamp. It may so happen that one box was CSB and the next box was Radio Banja Luka and that's why you get this different range of numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the sorting is done afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then thereafter they are replaced into the boxes and then they were scanned, although some scanning was done without the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Inayat, just for the record and to have a clear picture, try to follow me by referring to the chart that you have prepared. So we do have one batch from May of 1988?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I see that in box Z27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have -- yes, consisting of 37 pages; correct?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we have one batch from 1989. It's on the second page, referring to November, 1989?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's 84 pages?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then from 1991, we only have documents dated January, October and December of that year, and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. 344 plus one, plus 357?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then in 1992, the only month which is missing is October and it's missing completely? All the other months appear on the sheet?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1993, we only have January and February?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 1994, we only have October, on which you were asked by Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when you have nil on that chart, what does it mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this probably was a mistake committed by the data entry clerk, because when I was reading through the log sheet, I could see the complete range -- for example, let's take this example which is Z15, log number 8. And so this, Your Honours was all November, 1992, log number 7. And log number 8 was all December 1992. But these five documents, the data entry clerk probably forgot to mention the month and the year. I think it was just a mistake. So even though I have said "nil" here, I believe these are still belonging to months that are just preceding these numbers or just the ones that are following these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one final question: You just referred, for example, to this document, Z15, log number 8?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where you have B056842 to B056842, being one page?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the next line, you see that you start from 6843?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you continue the sequence?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you jump three, six, seven -- one moment. Let me find it. Yes, if you jump to six lines where you find five pages nil after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You start -- you see, you have a repetition of the same documents, and the line after, B001-4274, B001-4278, represent the five nil pages with the nil entry. And then you have a repetition. You don't have a continuation of the sequence as you had above, previously. You have B001-4274 again. You have those pages repeated here, which seems to confirm what Mr. Ackerman referred to previously, that there may be some pages which are repeated or scanned twice or entered or logged in twice.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first point that you have pointed out, 4274, going on to 4278, which is five pages, if you look at the next one, which is B0014274, in fact, my fault it should have been 4279, and then it goes on to 4472, so the last four digits are not the same as compared to the previous one that we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you deduct 4274 from 4472, it will leave you 198, you add the usual one and it brings you to 199, so the total pages would still remain correct but it's still repetition of five pages.

utterances.speaker: MAZHAR INAYAT [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, these are -- probably you have learned never to give me any statistics or any -- or any figures because I will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think anybody is going to claim it's a perfect, totally-without-fault system. It's the best that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need Mr. Inayat any longer? Yesterday I got the impression you intended to keep him here while you were referring to some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. What I would like to do is -- if Your Honours will allow me, to at the very least just go through the first lot of -- the first binder of the Banja Luka documents, just very quickly, looking at the documents that we have and while Mr. Inayat literally sits in the box, although I don't know if he has a binder so he better have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had misunderstood you yesterday, Ms. Korner. I thought we were going to work on binder 4. So I only asked for binder 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, binder 4 will be dealt with. It's military documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. That, I gathered. Yes. Yes. We are not going to have them all read, Mr. Ackerman. You will survive the day. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really have, I think, important things to say to you this morning about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If what Ms. Korner intends to do is read documents to you, I will sit here and bear that, but I will insist that she read every word in every document she's going to read to you, because otherwise, what she's doing is pointing out to you the portions of documents as to which she thinks you should pay particular attention and draw particular conclusions to. That is argument. The rules provide that comes at the end of the case. If what she intends to do is select from among the documents in that binder those which she thinks you should pay particular attention to and portions of those she thinks you should pay particular attention to, that again is argument and belongs at the end of the case according to the rules. If what she intends to do is show you the connections between documents and suggest you can draw certain conclusions by the way documents connect to each other, that's argument and according to the rules comes at the end of the case. If Your Honours permit her to make what amounts to argument at this point, I think you will be denying my client a fair trial and jeopardising the safety of any verdict that you arrive at at the end of this case, any judgement you arrive at at the end of this case. There are rules that provide when she can make argument and when she cannot, and she cannot serially argue this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, what do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents are as much part of the evidence as if I were calling a witness in the way that I have been calling and directing their attention to each of the parts of these documents. I can do this, and Mr. Ackerman, in my submission, would not be able to object, by saying to Mr. Inayat, "Mr. Inayat, I want you to look at this document here. Was it seized in 1997 or 1998 when the searches were conducted? Now, let's just have a look. Summarise the contents." Your Honour, I cannot see why that is argument or comment. It is putting into evidence those documents which are as much of importance in this particular case as if the witness was testifying about the events which have taken place. It is not argument. It is not comment. Your Honour, I can of course, if Mr. Ackerman insists, read out every word. I was proposing to - because we've covered a number of the documents - to summarise the contents of each of the documents so that Your Honours have a chance to have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Provided, Ms. Korner, that -- because I see the point raised by Mr. Ackerman, and I suppose you see it too. I mean, there's no question about it. One should definitely not take advantage of the opportunity to make reference to these documents in a way as to present arguments at this stage. That is definitely not -- not -- but that's not how I understood you were going to proceed. So more or less you have taken me a little bit by surprise, Mr. Ackerman, because I was not expecting Ms. Korner to embark upon this kind of exercise that you are objecting to. On the other hand, Ms. Korner is very right in maintaining that a document on its own, in itself, represents a piece of evidence. And being a piece of evidence, especially with a witness here that can answer question on -- answer questions on that piece of evidence in particular, she has every right now to take each and every document about which Mr. Inayat can provide an answer -- and provided that we do not embark on an exercise of reading these documents in part or in whole -- I mean, I sincerely hope that we -- that that is not what Ms. Korner means to do. And I take it that that's not what she means to do. I think we are perfectly regular in the procedure that we are adopting. And later on I would suppose that questions would be asked to witnesses about some or more of these documents. And this is what is important. You will immediately understand, Mr. Ackerman, that in actual fact, once these documents have been admitted in evidence, legally she has -- when I say -- the Prosecution has no obligation or absolute duty to examine -- to have each of these documents referred to one or more of the witnesses and have a statement made by one or more witnesses on those documents. I mean, I would imagine that several of these documents at the end of this trial would not have been referred to any witness at all. They would still be in the records of the case as exhibits, and the Trial Chamber is in duty bound to take them into consideration. So at this point in time, if Ms. Korner stands up and says, "Document P140," provided she does not build up an argument - there you are right - I cannot stop her at this point in time. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not sure you understand what it is she intends to do, Your Honour. But there is another problem. The other problem is this: There is a rule of this case that if she is going to present documents to a witness, we are supposed to be given a list well in advance of those documents. This morning she surprises us all, including you, that what she really intends to deal with is Banja Luka volume 1. I don't have Banja Luka volume 1 here. I can't carry every document in this case in and out of this courtroom every day. This is just totally and completely and utterly unfair, and it's -- it has the high potential of denying my client's right to a fair trial. It's the same thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please let me finish. It's the same thing as if I were to say to you, "Your Honours, I'm not certain that you paid as close attention to the testimony of the witnesses who have testified so far as I would have hoped you would; and therefore, I would like to go through the transcript for the next few hours pointing out to you the portions of the transcript that I think you ought to pay attention to." That's argument. That's what she intends to do this morning. And just because it's a document rather than testimony doesn't change its character as evidence. And I can't -- and the other thing is if there were a witness on the stand who's familiar with the contents of the document, then I can cross-examine. But he -- Mr. Inayat doesn't know anything about the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He wasn't there in 1992. We know he wasn't there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was there in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're not talking about searches any longer. We're talking about contents. She's trying to prove facts to you by making argument to you today. And the only thing I'll ask -- I understand you're going to permit it; it sounds to me like you are. The only thing I will ask is that you be patient with me objecting to everything she tries to do so I have a record that she is arguing this case to you at this point which is absolutely improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Inayat could only testify about the seizure of the documents and how the Prosecutor's office got hold of them. I don't think this can be contested. But all the other points that are important to do with the documents, Mr. Inayat cannot shed any light on this point, and we cannot cross-examine him on this. So I really do not see the point of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are pre-empting -- both you and Mr. Ackerman, you are pre-empting what the witness can or cannot state and you are also pre-empting what Ms. Korner is going to do or how she's going to handle this whole bundle and the next bundles. With regard to not having volume 1 available, I will give you time to have it available. I mean, there's no question about it. I mean, that's -- this is something that can be solved. But I don't think that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made it very clear yesterday - I appreciate Your Honours misunderstood - but that I wanted to go through the documents that hadn't been put into evidence through the witnesses yet or hadn't been referred to. Your Honour, I have yet to hear from Mr. Ackerman or Madam Fauveau what the unfairness to the defendants are. I am not going to comment on these documents. I am merely going to go through them summarising their contents -- and I do agree with Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau that it's unlikely Mr. Inayat can say anything about them other than obviously he was present at the time they were seized and in the course of the investigation, he's had a look at a lot of documents. But that doesn't -- I accept that doesn't take the case further. But I've yet to see what the unfairness is to the defendant. If Mr. Ackerman can point out the unfairness, then I'll willing listen to Your Honours have a look at the documents which were entered into evidence as admissible documents so that Your Honours know what those documents are. And that is -- as I say, that is part of the Prosecution case. And what is the difference, I ask rhetorically, if I were to call a witness to give evidence about matters which in this case are in written form contained in these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to Your Honours looking at all the documents. That's not what's trying to be done here. We're perfectly capable of looking at the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need your permission. We don't need your permission to look at the all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. So now she's saying what she wants to do is to have you look at the documents. Well, I trust you that you're going to do that, and I don't think it requires us to sit here and have her to tell you to look at a document. I think you will do that. I trust you to do that. To the extent -- to any extent that she wants to highlight the content of any document for your consideration, that is argument, pure and simple, and I object to it. It would take me a significant amount of time to go round up -- she hasn't told me what documents. If it's limited to volume 1, I can have volume 1 back here so I can follow her along maybe in 30 to 45 minutes. But I will insist on being able to have the documents, because it's unfair for her to be talking about documents that I can't even look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got nothing else to say in relation to what Mr. Ackerman complains about. The reason I would suggest he doesn't want Your Honours to have a look at it is because he knows that they're compelling evidence against his client. And this business of the trust, Your Honour, is just a method of avoiding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to why he hasn't got the volume here within this building, I cannot assist. It's required for him to go and get it. Or alternatively, we can supply him with another copy of volume 1. We do have spare copies. And indeed, if Madam Fauveau hasn't got hers either, we'll do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor can provide me a copy of the documents, I will agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I still haven't understood how Mr. Ackerman can argue that if Ms. Korner stands up and takes documents -- I'll take this one -- a document P134 and says, "Your Honours, this is a document forming part of the bundle seized from Banja Luka Radio Station, and it deals with a report on such and such a thing. The Prosecution is only -- attaches importance only to this," how does that become argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's clearly argument. "Please look at paragraph 6 of this document, Your Honour. We contend that this is the important one." That's argument. The other thing -- we might as well excuse Mr. Inayat because he obviously has no role in this. All he can do is say, "Yes, I've seen that document." We have already accepted the sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have accepted the sources. But if Ms. Korner needs Mr. Inayat, I'm not going to send him out. It depends as we go along, the utility of his presence, whether it emerges really a reality or whether it's just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just don't think it's fair for there to be--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, it's up to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's fair for us to be creating an illusion that this is testimony from a witness. It's not. It's a speech from Ms. Korner with regard the documents. And if you want to permit it, I can't stop it. I'll sit here and listen to it. But it's extremely unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it puts your client in an advantageous position in knowing beforehand, well beforehand, what importance, if at all, the Prosecution is attaching to the various exhibits that have already been admitted so that in due course you can direct your attention where these documents would require you to direct your attention. I mean, it's -- rather than being unfair, it's a mode of discovery and disclosure that enables you to prepare better for your defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, document number P74 is dated the 8th of July.
